briefing.headline: Pick the editor everyone else uses.
body: VS Code is the editor. Free, fast, the most popular editor among working developers by a wide margin. Cursor is built on top of it. The keyboard shortcuts you learn here transfer to most other editors you'll ever touch.

Setup is fast. What takes longer — and what this module barely touches — is internalizing the shortcuts. Don't worry about that yet. Get it installed, get the integrated terminal working, learn the Command Palette. The rest you'll pick up by using it.

reference.title: Essential keyboard shortcuts
reference.content:
Cmd + P              Quick file open
Cmd + Shift + P      Command Palette
Cmd + B              Toggle sidebar
Cmd + `              Toggle terminal
Cmd + /              Comment current line
Cmd + D              Select next match (multi-cursor)
Cmd + Shift + F      Search across files
Cmd + ,              Open settings

reference.title: What the Command Palette is
reference.content: Cmd + Shift + P opens a search bar that runs every command in VS Code — including ones added by extensions. If you can't remember a keyboard shortcut, type what you want here. This is the most useful single shortcut in the editor.

reference.title: Open from the terminal
reference.content:
code .              Open current directory in VS Code
code myfile.js      Open one file
code ~/projects     Open a specific folder

reference.title: Extensions worth installing
reference.content: Prettier — automatic code formatting. GitLens — see who wrote any line and when. ESLint — catches common JavaScript mistakes (install when you start writing JS). Skip everything else until you have a reason to install it.

reference.title: "command not found: code"
reference.content: You skipped the "Install the code command" step, or didn't restart your terminal after. Open the Command Palette (Cmd + Shift + P) and run Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH. Then close and reopen iTerm2.

completion.headline: M2 complete.
completion.body: You have a working editor with terminal, extensions, and shortcuts. Next up: M3 — Git & GitHub.

steps.title: Install VS Code
steps.body: Free, official, made by Microsoft. Don't pay for anything else.
notes: Go to code.visualstudio.com and click Download for Mac
Open the downloaded .zip — Visual Studio Code appears
Drag Visual Studio Code into your Applications folder
Open it: Cmd + Space → "Visual Studio Code" → Enter
If macOS asks to confirm a downloaded app: click Open
steps.verify: VS Code is open. You see a Welcome tab.

steps.title: Install the code command
steps.body: Adds a code command to your terminal. Now you can open any folder in VS Code with one command from iTerm2.
notes: In VS Code, press Cmd + Shift + P to open the Command Palette
Type: shell command
Click Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH
Enter your Mac password if prompted
steps.verify: Open iTerm2 and run code --version. It prints a version number.
steps.trouble: If command not found: code — close and reopen iTerm2. Shell needs to reload.

steps.title: Open a folder from the terminal
steps.body: The most common way to start work: cd into a folder, then code . to open it. The dot means "current directory."
steps.code:
cd ~
mkdir vscode-practice
cd vscode-practice
code .
steps.verify: VS Code opens with vscode-practice as the project folder. The Explorer (left sidebar) shows it's empty.

steps.title: Tour the interface
notes: Activity Bar (far left, vertical icons): switch between Explorer, Search, Source Control, Run, Extensions.
Side Bar: contents of whichever Activity Bar icon is selected — usually the Explorer (your file tree).
Editor (center): where you edit files. Multiple tabs.
Panel (bottom, hidden until needed): integrated terminal, problems, output. Toggle with Cmd + `.
Status Bar (very bottom): current branch, errors, file encoding, line and column.
steps.verify: You can identify each region. Toggle the sidebar with Cmd + B and the panel with Cmd + `.

steps.title: Use the integrated terminal
steps.body: VS Code has a terminal built in. Same zsh, same Homebrew, same everything as iTerm2 — just inside the editor. Most developers stop using their separate terminal app for project work and live here.
notes: Press Cmd + ` to open the terminal panel.
Run pwd — it prints the path to vscode-practice.
Run touch hello.js — the file appears in the Explorer immediately.
Click hello.js in the Explorer to open it in the editor.
steps.verify: hello.js exists, is visible in the Explorer, and is open in the editor.

steps.title: Command Palette
steps.body: Cmd + Shift + P. Single most useful shortcut in VS Code. Every command — built-in or from extensions — is searchable here. When you don't know a shortcut, type what you want.
notes: Press Cmd + Shift + P.
Type "format" — see all formatting commands.
Press Escape.
Press Cmd + Shift + P again, type "theme", select Color Theme, pick one. Try Default Dark Modern or one of the Light themes.
steps.verify: VS Code's color theme has changed.

steps.title: Quick file open
steps.body: Cmd + P opens any file in the project by name. Fuzzy-matched — type a few letters and it finds it. Use this instead of clicking through the Explorer once a project gets bigger than a handful of files.
notes: Press Cmd + P.
Type hello.
Press Enter to open hello.js.

steps.title: Multi-cursor
steps.body: Edit multiple places at once. Cmd + D selects the next occurrence of whatever you've highlighted — keep pressing to add more. Then type once and it changes everywhere.
notes: Open hello.js.

Type these three lines:
let foo = 1;
let foo = 2;
let foo = 3;
Double-click one of the foos to select it.
Press Cmd + D twice — the next two foos are also selected.
Type bar — all three change at once.
Press Escape to exit multi-cursor.
steps.verify: All three lines now say let bar = N;.

steps.title: Search across files
steps.body: Cmd + Shift + F searches every file in the project. Different from Cmd + F, which searches only the current file.
notes: Press Cmd + Shift + F.
Type bar.
Click a result to jump to it.
steps.verify: Search panel shows matches with file names. Clicking a match jumps you to the line.

steps.title: Install essential extensions
steps.body: Extensions add features. The two below are nearly universal — most developers run both.
notes: Click the Extensions icon in the Activity Bar (square with one block detached) — or press Cmd + Shift + X.
Search Prettier - Code formatter. Install the one by Prettier.
Search GitLens. Install the one by GitKraken.
Restart VS Code if prompted.
steps.verify: Both extensions show "Uninstall" instead of "Install" — meaning they're active.

steps.title: Format on save
steps.body: Have Prettier reformat your code automatically every time you save. Stops you from arguing with yourself about whitespace.
notes: Open settings: Cmd + ,.
Search format on save.
Check the Editor: Format On Save box.
Search default formatter.
Set Editor: Default Formatter to Prettier - Code formatter.
steps.verify: Open hello.js, mess up the indentation, save (Cmd + S) — Prettier fixes it.

steps.title: Clean up
steps.body: Delete the practice folder. The Welcome tab is enough — you don't need a leftover empty project sitting in your home directory.
steps.verify: Folder is gone. Close the VS Code window — the project is no longer accessible.
